transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
Cornell University has named a former leader of the Justice Department to head an investigation
into how the school handles reports of sexual assault.
NPR's Jacqueline Diaz reports that includes the school's response to a woman who alleges
she was gang-raped at Cornell two years ago.
Former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates will lead the internal review into how
Cornell responded when the now former student reported being drugged and repeatedly raped
at a fraternity on campus.
Yates was picked by a newly formed special committee of the Cornell University Board
of Trustees.
She will also examine the school's policies on how it prevents in response to sexual harassment,
assault, and other misconduct on campus.
This all comes after a former student filed a lawsuit against the school last month.
The student, who goes by Jane Doe, alleges failings in how Cornell administrators handled
her case.
Yates' probe is separate from a reopening of the criminal case, which is being led by
New York AG Letitia James.
Jacqueline Diaz, NPR News.
A source tells NPR that the reason the U.S. military withdrew its bombers from a base
in the U.K. was because of a threat of an Iranian drone attack.
NPR's Quill Lawrence reports the U.S. removed all 12 of its B-1 bombers.
A U.S. government official, not authorized to speak publicly, confirmed to NPR that fears
of a drone attack on behalf of Iran caused the U.S. to withdraw all the American bombers
from Fairford Air Base in England.
The base has been used for bombing sorties in the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran.
Late last month, British authorities arrested five men traveling in white vans near the
air base in the pre-dawn hours.
The men were later released after no explosives were found.
British officials say the men remain under investigation, and two more arrests have been
made in the past week, including a British-Iranian dual national.
Quill Lawrence, NPR News.
A new poll out today shows Democrats have a nearly two-to-one edge over Republicans
when it comes to voter trust on health care costs, and PR's Selena Simmons-Duffin reports.
The cost of health care is weighing heavily on voters' minds with the midterm elections
just one month away.
That's according to the new poll from KFF, a nonpartisan health research organization.
KFF's Ashley Kurzinger says they polled 1,300 people in mid-September.
What we are seeing is that the Democratic Party has the advantage overall among all
voters on which party voters trust to handle health care, but they also have the advantage
among independent voters, and that's a really important voting bloc for midterm elections.
Kurzinger says Democrats had a 10-point advantage on health costs in April.
Now that gap has doubled.
22% of voters trust Republicans on the issue, compared to 42% who trust Democrats.
Selena Simmons-Duffin, NPR News, Washington.
The U.S. stock market hit an all-time high today.
The S&P 500 climbed more than half a percent, topping its record set in August.
This is NPR.
Donald Trump has pledged to use money from his MAGA Inc. super PAC for an ad campaign
that has so far been funded by taxpayers, but he hasn't committed to reimbursing the
nearly $12 million already spent.
Trump said today, quote, "will decide" whether to repay the funds.
Members of both parties have criticized the ads.
Legal experts say they might not be legal.
The White House defends them as public service announcements.
Former televangelist Jim Baker, who built and lost a religious and media empire based
in South Carolina, has died.
He was 86.
From South Carolina Public Radio, Scott Morgan reports.
Baker and his late wife Tammy Faye built the PTL, or Praise the Lord, club into a television
powerhouse in the 1980s.
In daily one-hour broadcasts from Heritage USA and Fort Mill, the Bakers reached millions
of viewers and hosted thousands of visitors to the Christian-themed hotel and park just
a few miles south of Charlotte.
But Baker had been the subject of financial investigators dating back to the late '70s.
The couple had built an evangelical empire that preached prosperity and celebrated conspicuous
consumption.
But that empire unraveled in the wake of sex crime accusations and hush money payments
for Jim Baker's accuser, Secretary Jessica Hahn, in 1987.
Two years later, Baker was convicted of fraud connected to memberships to Heritage USA.
He was sentenced to 45 years in federal prison.
For NPR News, I'm Scott Morgan in Columbia, South Carolina.
Connecticut officials are advising people on building unwelcome mats, that is electrified
doormats meant to keep bears away amid an uptick in bear encounters.
Components include a rubber mat, a metal screen, and an electric fence energizer.
This is NPR News from Washington.

topics.text: Cornell University names former Acting Attorney General Sally Yates to investigate sexual assault handling
U.S. military withdrew 12 B-1 bombers from England base due to Iranian drone attack threat
Democrats hold nearly two-to-one polling advantage over Republicans on voter trust regarding health care costs
U.S. stock market S&P 500 reaches all-time high, climbing more than half a percent
Donald Trump pledges MAGA Inc. super PAC funds for ad campaign but won't commit to reimbursement
Former televangelist Jim Bakker, PTL Club founder, dies at age 86 in South Carolina
Connecticut officials recommend electrified doormats to keep bears away amid increase in bear encounters
